lead: Private-key cryptography, also called symmetric cryptography, hides a message by mixing it with a secret key that sender and receiver already share. The readable message is plaintext m, the scrambled message is ciphertext c, and the shared secret is key k. Encryption is c = E_k(m); decryption is m = D_k(c). A correct cipher recovers every message exactly. This model protects bulk data in UPI payments, messaging apps and encrypted disks because it is fast. Its weak point is key distribution: both sides must obtain the same secret without an eavesdropper learning it.
prereq: You need only basic probability and binary arithmetic.

blocks.text: Private-key cryptography, also called symmetric cryptography, uses one secret key k for both directions. The sender turns plaintext m into ciphertext c with encryption c = E_k(m). The receiver turns c back into m with decryption m = D_k(c). Correctness means D_k(E_k(m)) = m for every allowed message. The set of possible keys is the key space. Security must not depend on hiding the algorithm: assume the enemy knows E and D and only k is secret (Kerckhoffs's principle). If an attacker learns k, all messages protected by that key become readable. Only a few universities teach this as a full topic; in quantum computing it is the classical baseline. Private-key ciphers are fast, so they encrypt the bulk of network traffic. The key must be generated randomly and kept secret. The figure shows the same key at both ends.

sections.h3: Perfect secrecy and the one-time pad

blocks.text: Perfect secrecy is the strongest definition. A cipher has perfect secrecy when seeing c tells an attacker nothing new about m: P(m | c) = P(m) for every message m and ciphertext c. The one-time pad achieves this. Write the message as a bit string m, choose a key k of the same length, with each key bit independent and equally likely 0 or 1. Encryption is bitwise XOR, c = m ⊕ k; decryption is m = c ⊕ k, because XOR with the same bit twice returns the original bit. If k is uniform, c is uniform and independent of m. For a one-time pad the key is as long as the message, so a 1 MB file needs a 1 MB key. Some syllabi call this the Vernam cipher. The conditions are strict: k random, same length as m, and used once only. Reuse leaks m₁⊕m₂ and destroys perfect secrecy.
c = m ⊕ k,   m = c ⊕ k
blocks.where: m is the plaintext bit string; k is the random key bit string of the same length; c is the ciphertext; ⊕ is bitwise XOR.

blocks.text: Block ciphers handle data in fixed-size chunks. DES encrypts 64-bit blocks with a 56-bit key; the key is too short for modern brute force. AES encrypts 128-bit blocks with a 128-, 192- or 256-bit key and is the current standard. A block cipher encrypts one block, so modes of operation chain blocks for long files. These ciphers aim at computational security: breaking them should take too much time, not be impossible in principle. They do not have perfect secrecy because one key is reused across blocks. The practical weak point is key distribution: n users needing pairwise private keys need n(n−1)/2 keys, each delivered safely. Public-key methods such as RSA and Diffie–Hellman reduce this problem, but are slower; they usually agree a private key for AES. Quantum key distribution in 5.2 attacks the same problem with physics.

figure.caption: Alice XORs m=1011 with k=0110 bit by bit to get c=1101. Bob uses the same k=0110 on c, and the bottom row returns m=1011.

spec.title: XOR with k=0110
spec.aria: Plaintext bits 1011 XOR with key 0110 give ciphertext 1101; XORing 1101 with the same key 0110 gives back 1011.

examples.question: Alice and Bob share a 4-bit one-time-pad key k=0110. Alice sends m=1011. Compute c=m⊕k and show Bob recovers m.
steps: Check in decimal: 13⊕6=11, the original message.
examples.check:
m = 0b1011
k = 0b0110
c = m ^ k
rec = c ^ k
print(c)
print(rec)

traps: Reusing a one-time-pad key leaks c₁⊕c₂=m₁⊕m₂. The pad must be random, message-length and used once.
AES and DES are not perfectly secret; they give computational security and need a mode for long messages.
Private-key means one shared secret; public-key (RSA, Diffie–Hellman) uses a key pair and is only contrast here.
In c=m⊕k, ⊕ is bitwise XOR, not addition. Align bits and keep leading zeros.

quiz.q: Define plaintext m, ciphertext c and shared key k in a private-key cipher.
quiz.a: m is the readable message; c is the encrypted message; k is the secret used in E_k and D_k.

quiz.q: State perfect secrecy in one equation.
quiz.a: P(m | c) = P(m) for every message m and ciphertext c: c gives no new information about m.

quiz.q: With m=1100 and one-time-pad k=1010, compute c=m⊕k and recover m.
Why is reusing a one-time-pad key unsafe? Give the leaked combination.
quiz.a: Two ciphertexts give c₁⊕c₂=(m₁⊕k)⊕(m₂⊕k)=m₁⊕m₂, which links the two messages and removes the key.

quiz.q: Compare DES and AES by block size and key size.
quiz.a: DES uses 64-bit blocks and a 56-bit key; AES uses 128-bit blocks and 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys.

quiz.q: For n=10 users needing pairwise private keys, how many keys are needed and why is distribution hard?
quiz.a: n(n−1)/2=10×9/2=45 keys; each pair needs a separate secret delivered safely, so the number grows as n².

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems use hybrid encryption: a public-key step agrees a session key, then AES-GCM encrypts data. Search for AES-GCM, Kerckhoffs's principle and the one-time-pad proof; 5.2 replaces unsafe key delivery with physics.
